content.thinking:
Eric's pointing out that the belief rows on the /lab contents page are confusing without context—they mix first and second person quotes like developer misconceptions, but nothing on the page explains that these are beliefs developers hold. Someone landing directly on /lab via a shared link would just see odd disconnected sentences with no framing.

The "one chapter at a time, in public" line also feels out of place—that's roadmap/landing page framing, not what a contents-page visitor needs. I need to rewrite the standfirst to actually explain the scheme: each chapter title is something developers say or believe, and the chapter runs the real feature against it. I have to be careful with voice.md's rule against "labeling the confrontation"—that governs individual exhibits, not an index explaining its own titling convention—but I still shouldn't use words like "misconceptions" or "things everyone gets wrong."

The landing page copy already nails this without calling anything wrong: "something developers are sure about... runs the real feature next to it" covers the quote format and the I/You mix while staying covert, letting the panel itself deliver the verdict. I'm drafting standfirst options along these lines, considering whether to reuse that phrasing closely or vary it, and weighing a possible second sentence pointing to the source drawer.

I'm keeping the scope sentence about covering everything Next.js can do plus whatever Vercel claims can be proven from inside a web page, since it sets up the shelf list well, and dropping the "one chapter at a time, in public" line per Eric's note. Now I'm testing a draft standfirst combining both ideas, then running it through voice passes — the first attempt feels too explain-y, so I'm trying alternate phrasing that keeps the quoted belief and the I/You framing without over-explaining it.

I'm working through how to frame the mix of I-titles (self-talk) and You-titles (advice from a reviewer), since that's what confused Eric. I try a version that names the confrontation directly — "right before the feature proves otherwise" — but that announces the gotcha too openly, violating the covert tone rule, so I'm sticking with the subtler landing: "...and runs the real feature next to it."

I'm settling on dropping the "in public" clause entirely, landing on the final version: chapters open on something developers say to themselves or each other, then run the real feature alongside it, with the plan being everything Next.js can do plus whatever of Vercel can be proven from inside a page. I'm double-checking that "every chapter" accurately refers to the shipped chapters versus the planned topic rows.

I'm also checking the /lab metadata description stays as-is since it's unaffected, and confirming the landing page's roadmap section is the right place to keep the "one chapter at a time, in public" framing since it sits next to the built-in-the-open aside — so I'll leave that alone and just edit the lab page's standfirst text.

This reveals a genuine new finding worth logging: an index page of beliefs needs its framing stated once, since the contents page is a bare list without context. I'm adding a dated evidence row to §6 documenting this, starting to draft the table.

Now I'll implement the fix: edit the page standfirst, append to voice.md, build, run a curl check, then commit and push.

content.text: He's right on both counts: the belief titles explain themselves next to a running exhibit, but as a bare index they're just odd quotes in mixed persons — the contents page has to state the titling frame once. And the in-public line belongs where the making-of lives (the landing roadmap), not here. The fix, drafted through the passes, leans on the Ford stance to explain the I/You mix without labeling the confrontation:

> *Every chapter opens on something developers say — to ourselves, or to each other — and runs the real feature next to it. The plan is everything Next.js can do, and as much of Vercel as can be proved from inside a web page.*

Both complaints resolved by one sentence. The first clause states the titling frame a cold visitor needs: the rows are *sayings*, and "to ourselves, or to each other" quietly accounts for the mixed persons — the I-titles are self-talk ("I'll put 'use client' on it, to be safe"), the You-titles are advice received ("You need an API route for that"). It's the Ford stance doing the explaining — *ourselves* includes the narrator — so the frame lands without labeling anyone wrong, which keeps voice.md §4's rule intact: the verdict still belongs to the panels, not the index. And "One chapter at a time, in public" is gone from the contents page — that framing lives where the making-of does, on the landing roadmap with its built-in-the-open aside, and it stays there.

The diagnosis earned a voice.md §6 entry, because no existing rule predicted it: **beside a running exhibit, a belief title explains itself; as a bare index it doesn't — an index of beliefs states its titling frame once.** That's now recorded with the rejected standfirst as evidence, dated, in chronological position. Verified on the production build: the new frame renders, the in-public line is absent.

content.thinking:
Eric needs an Impressum and Datenschutzerklärung for hasToggle.dev that satisfy German legal requirements but are written in English, with placeholders for personal data, using adsimple.de's generator as a structural reference. I'm checking the existing legal page infrastructure, which already renders MDX content for privacy and terms pages under `/legal/[slug]`.

Now I'm working through the actual legal requirements: the Impressum obligations stem from § 5 DDG (which replaced TMG § 5 in 2024) plus § 18 MStV, requiring the provider's name, a loadable address, email, and a secondary fast contact method like phone.

I also need to note that the EU ODR platform was shut down in July 2025, so that link shouldn't be included anymore, though the VSBG § 36 dispute-resolution declaration still applies. Since hasToggle runs a paid cohort, it counts as geschäftsmäßig, so an Impressum is definitely required.

For the privacy section, I'm covering GDPR Art. 13/14 duties: controller identity, purposes and legal bases, recipients including third-country transfers since Vercel is US-based (DPF/SCCs), storage duration, data subject rights, and the right to complain to the relevant German authority. I also need a hosting section specifically addressing Vercel's server logs and IP collection.

Now I'm thinking through cookies and local storage under the new TDDDG (formerly TTDSG) — technically necessary storage like theme preferences is exempt, but I need to inventory what the site actually processes to make sure the privacy policy matches reality: Vercel hosting with its third-country transfer implications, and Vercel Web Analytics which is cookie-free but still counts as processing.

I also need to check whether Speed Insights, PostHog, and Google Analytics are actually active in production versus just included in the codebase, plus account for Sentry error tracking and the digest signup flow — email collection via consent with double opt-in, using Resend (a US processor) and MongoDB for storage.

MongoDB Atlas is hosted in Frankfurt based on earlier GDPR work. The contact form collects name, email, and message. I'm noting the cookies actually set in practice: a functional demo cookie from the mutation playground and a localStorage theme preference, both exempt under § 25 Abs. 2 TDDDG but worth documenting transparently. Fonts are self-hosted rather than pulled from Google Fonts, which is good and avoids needing a separate disclosure section.

I'm also checking whether YouTube/X embeds or third-party services like Liveblocks, Knock, and Stripe are actually active on the web surface versus just existing as packages — Stripe seems app/API-only, not web-facing, so the privacy policy should focus on the current site with placeholders for future cohort payment features. On language, I'm weighing whether English-only is legally defensible for a site targeting international developers, concluding it's a reasonable choice worth flagging to Eric as a deliberate decision.

Now I'm planning to check the existing privacy.mdx and terms.mdx files to see if they're boilerplate, then replace privacy.mdx content and create a new imprint.mdx using "Imprint" as the title and slug since that's the common English term for Impressum — leaving terms.mdx untouched since Eric only asked for imprint and privacy.

For reachability, German law requires the Impressum be easily recognizable and directly accessible from every page, so I'm planning to add small "Imprint · Privacy" links into the footer's bottom trademark row rather than creating a whole new sitemap column, since that satisfies the legal requirement while staying subtle and consistently present.

I should double-check a few recent legal details since my knowledge cutoff might miss 2024-2025 changes — things like the DDG §5 status, the ODR platform shutdown, TDDDG naming, and VSBG — and also glance at adsimple's generator structure for its section list as a reference. Then I'll draft the two MDX files using placeholder fields like full name, address, email, phone, VAT ID, and supervisory authority for the user to fill in.

For voice, legal pages need precise, plain language rather than the playful tone used elsewhere — though GDPR Art. 12 actually requires clear and plain language, so a straightforward, honest register is both stylistically and legally appropriate here, with maybe one warm intro sentence but no jokes in the substantive legal text. I also want to confirm the legal slugs and sitemap generation work automatically from the files so the imprint page appears without extra wiring.

Next I'll search for current German Impressumspflicht requirements under § 5 DDG and check whether the EU ODR platform reference is still valid for 2025, then look at an existing generator page for structural reference. I'll also review the current legal MDX files and the legal slug page, verify which analytics providers are actually active, and then write the updated imprint and privacy pages along with footer links before checking the build.

Based on the search results, here's information about Impressum requirements under § 5 DDG for individual entrepreneurs and website requirements in 2025:

## Impressumspflicht nach § 5 DDG

The impressum obligation under § 5 DDG applies to all providers of business-like digital services, meaning that almost every website with a commercial background should have an impressum.

## Anforderungen für Einzelunternehmer

For individual entrepreneurs specifically, the first and last name of the business owner must be provided, with the business name being optional. This includes individual entrepreneurs and traders with their own website or landing page.

## Pflichtangaben (Required Information)

Each commercial website requires an impressum with the full name, postal address, email plus a second quick contact method, for companies the legal form, authorized representatives and registration number, as well as the VAT ID (if available).

## Website-Anforderungen (Website Requirements)

The information must be easily recognizable and directly accessible, meaning the impressum should be accessible from the homepage, ideally via a clearly labeled link such as "Impressum" or "Kontakt". It must be reachable from each page with a maximum of two clicks.

The impressum and privacy policy are two separate mandatory disclosures that should be on separate pages and each be accessible via their own link.

## Zusätzliche Anforderungen (Additional Requirements)

Since the implementation of the Barrierefreiheitsstärkungsgesetz (BFSG) in June 2025, many websites have additional accessibility requirements.

title: "Privacy Policy"
description: "How we handle your data"

## Overview

This Privacy Policy describes how has-toggle ("we", "us", or "our") collects, uses, and shares your personal information when you use our services.

## Information We Collect

We collect information you provide directly, such as when you create an account, use our services, or contact us for support.

### Account Information

When you create an account, we collect your name, email address, and password.

### Usage Data

We automatically collect information about how you interact with our services, including pages visited, features used, and actions taken.

## How We Use Your Information

We use your information to:

- Provide, maintain, and improve our services
- Send you technical notices and support messages
- Respond to your comments and questions

## Contact Us

If you have questions about this Privacy Policy, please contact us at privacy@hastoggle.dev.

**The imprint** (`/legal/imprint`) follows **§ 5 DDG** — the Impressumspflicht moved from the old TMG to the Digital Services Act in 2024: your full name and a *servable* postal address (no P.O. box), email **plus a second fast contact channel** (I put a phone placeholder — case law wobbles on alternatives, a number ends the argument), a VAT-ID section (deletable if none is assigned), the **§ 18 (2) MStV** responsible-person block — required because the blog and write-ups are editorial content — and the **§ 36 VSBG** declaration of non-participation in consumer arbitration. One thing deliberately *absent*: the EU ODR platform link that lived in every German imprint since 2016 — the platform was shut down on July 20, 2025 and the regulation repealed, so references must be removed, not added.

**The privacy policy** (`/legal/privacy`) follows GDPR Art. 13 plus the TDDDG, and — the part that matters most — **matches what the site actually runs**, which I inventoried first: Vercel hosting (Frankfurt functions) and cookieless Web Analytics, Arcjet request screening, Sentry error reports, the digest (double opt-in, consent basis, one-click unsubscribe), the contact form, **exactly one cookie** (`playground-presses`, functional under § 25 (2) TDDDG — the policy names the demo cookie, which is very on-brand truth), theme in localStorage, self-hosted fonts. It opens with a plain-language "short version" — Art. 12 requires clear language, so for once the house style is legally mandated — and closes with the full rights catalog including the supervisory-authority complaint (authority is a placeholder by Bundesland). Structure mirrors what the adsimple-class generators produce, in English.

**Wiring:** footer gains **Imprint · Privacy** in the bottom line (every page, two-click rule), and the legal layout now renders the footer so those pages aren't dead ends. Sitemap picks the new slug up automatically. All concrete data is `[bracketed]`; fill-in guidance sits in MDX comments that never render — verified invisible in the served HTML.

**Four things flagged for you, not decided:** (1) the MDX comments mark several *verify* items — Sentry data region, Arcjet's transfer mechanism, Resend's address, MongoDB region, contact-message destination, DPA links — confirm each when you fill the brackets; (2) if `NEXT_PUBLIC_GA_MEASUREMENT_ID` is ever set in production, Google Analytics needs a consent section *and a banner* — a warning comment guards that spot; (3) English-only legal pages are common and defensible for an international-audience site, but bilingual is the risk-averse option for a Germany-based operator — your call; (4) `terms.mdx` is still next-forge boilerplate mentioning accounts that don't exist — worth deleting or rewriting when the cohort makes real terms necessary.

Sources: [IHK Chemnitz — Impressumspflicht](https://www.ihk.de/chemnitz/recht-und-steuern/rechtsinformationen/internetrecht/pflichtangaben-im-internet-die-impressumspflicht-4401580), [eRecht24 — Impressumspflicht](https://www.e-recht24.de/artikel/datenschutz/209.html), [Impressumspflicht nach § 5 DDG](https://service-rechtsschutz.de/die-impressumspflicht-nach-%C2%A7-5-ddg/), [iubenda — ODR platform discontinuation](https://www.iubenda.com/en/blog/discontinuation-of-the-european-online-dispute-resolution-odr-platform/), [nbs partners — ODR shutdown actions](https://www.nbs-partners.de/en/latest-news/discontinuation-of-the-eu-online-dispute-resolution-platform-on-20-july-2025-essential-information-and-actions-for-businesses/).

Sections marked "delete if…" describe services that may not be active — the policy must always match what the site actually runs. */} Last updated: [date] ## Controller The controller responsible for processing on this website (hastoggle.dev) is: **[Full name]**
[Street and house number]
[Postal code] [City]
Germany Email: [email address] ## The short version This site has no accounts, no advertising, and no cross-site tracking. Most of it is static pages with running demos. What does get processed: server logs when pages are delivered, cookieless usage statistics, error reports when something breaks, an email address if you sign up for the Monday digest, and whatever you write us through the contact form. One demo sets one cookie, and it says so right next to the button. The details, legal bases and your rights follow below. ## Legal bases Where this policy names a legal basis, it refers to Art. 6 (1) GDPR: - **(a) consent** — you actively agreed, and can withdraw at any time; - **(b) contract** — processing is needed to do the thing you asked for; - **(f) legitimate interest** — running this site securely and reliably. For storing or reading information on your device (cookies, local storage), § 25 TDDDG applies; this site only uses storage that is strictly necessary for a function you use (§ 25 (2) TDDDG), so no consent banner is required. ## Hosting This site is hosted by **Vercel Inc.**, 650 California St, San Francisco, CA 94108, USA. When you open a page, Vercel processes the technical data every web server needs: your IP address, the requested URL, date and time, transferred data volume, referrer, and user-agent. This happens in server logs, on the legal basis of our legitimate interest (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR) in delivering the site securely. Server-side functions run in Vercel's Frankfurt region; static content is delivered by Vercel's global edge network. Vercel is certified under the EU–US Data Privacy Framework; a data processing agreement is in place. [Verify: link Vercel's DPA] ## Rate limiting and security To keep automated abuse off the site, requests are screened by **Arcjet, Inc.** [Arcjet address], which processes the IP address and technical request characteristics for the moment of the decision. Legal basis: legitimate interest (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR) in protecting the service. [Verify: Arcjet DPA / transfer mechanism; delete this section if Arcjet is not active in production.] ## Error monitoring When something on the site crashes, an error report is sent to **Sentry** (Functional Software, Inc., 45 Fremont Street, San Francisco, CA 94105, USA), containing the technical context of the error — which may include your IP address, user-agent, and the state of the page at the time. Legal basis: legitimate interest (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR) in finding and fixing defects. IP addresses are not used to identify visitors. [Verify: Sentry data region + DPA; Sentry offers EU data residency — state which is configured.] ## Usage statistics This site uses **Vercel Web Analytics**, which counts page views and interactions without cookies and without persistent identifiers: visitors are distinguished by a short-lived hash that cannot be traced across sites or days. No advertising IDs, no cross-site profiles. Legal basis: legitimate interest (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR) in knowing which pages are read. {/* GOOGLE ANALYTICS — the codebase can load GA when NEXT_PUBLIC_GA_MEASUREMENT_ID is set. If it is set in production, a GA section with consent handling (Art. 6 (1) (a), § 25 (1) TDDDG) is REQUIRED here — and a consent banner with it, because GA is not "strictly necessary". If GA stays off, leave this comment as a warning and ship no GA section. As of 2026-08-21 the provider only renders GA when the key exists. */} ## Cookies and local storage This site sets exactly one cookie: `playground-presses`, an `httpOnly` cookie holding the press count of the Server Actions demo — it exists so the demo can prove a point about cookies your JavaScript cannot read, and it is functional storage under § 25 (2) TDDDG. It expires [verify: session / max-age] and identifies nothing but a number. Your theme choice (light, dark, or system) is kept in your browser's local storage, never sent to us. Fonts are self-hosted; no requests go to font CDNs. ## The Monday digest If you sign up for the weekly email, we process your email address — nothing else — to send you the digest. Signup is double opt-in: you get a confirmation email, and only a confirmed address is ever written to the list. We store the address, the confirmation status, and its timestamps in our database ([verify: MongoDB Atlas, Frankfurt/EU region]); emails are sent through **Resend** ([Resend Inc. address], USA) as our processor. Legal basis: your consent (Art. 6 (1) (a) GDPR). Every email contains an unsubscribe link; unsubscribing is one click, it works the first time, and your address is then deleted from the list. Legal basis: Art. 6 (1) (b) GDPR where your message concerns a contract or pre-contractual question, otherwise our legitimate interest in answering (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR). To exercise any of these, one email to [email address] is enough. content.text:
Here's the complete fill-in map. Everything sits in two files — `apps/web/content/legal/imprint.mdx` and `apps/web/content/legal/privacy.mdx` — and every spot is marked either as a `[bracketed placeholder]` in the visible text or flagged by an invisible `{/* … */}` comment right beside it. Three tiers:

**1. Data only you can provide — fill the brackets**

In **imprint.mdx**:
- **Provider** — full name, street + house number, postal code + city. (If you operate under a registered business name, it goes above your personal name; otherwise your name alone satisfies § 5 DDG.)
- **Contact** — email, and a phone number (the legally required *second* fast channel).
- **VAT ID** — your `DE…` USt-IdNr., or delete the whole section if none is assigned (a comment explains the Wirtschafts-ID alternative).
- **Responsible for editorial content** — name + address; may simply repeat the provider block.

In **privacy.mdx**:
- **"Last updated: [date]"** at the top — set when you finalize.
- **Controller** — the same identity block plus email.
- **Your rights** — the contact email appears once more ("one email to […] is enough"), and the **competent supervisory authority** of your Bundesland with address and link (e.g. Bavaria → BayLDA, NRW → LDI NRW, Berlin → BlnBDI — it's determined by where you're established).

**2. Facts to verify in your accounts — each marked `[Verify: …]` in privacy.mdx**
- **Hosting** — link Vercel's DPA and confirm their Data Privacy Framework certification is current.
- **Rate limiting** — is `ARCJET_KEY` actually set in production? If not, delete the Arcjet section; if yes, add Arcjet's address and DPA/transfer mechanism.
- **Error monitoring** — which Sentry data region your project uses (US default vs. EU residency) and their DPA; the sentence adjusts either way.
- **The digest** — confirm the MongoDB Atlas region for *this* database (your earlier GDPR work used Frankfurt — verify it holds for the subscribers collection), Resend's postal address, and what unsubscribe actually does (hard delete vs. suppression-list retention — the policy currently promises deletion).
- **Contact form** — where messages actually land (which inbox/provider), named as a processor if applicable.
- **Recipients & transfers / Storage duration** — DPA links per provider and concrete retention windows (Vercel log retention, Sentry event retention).

The cookie-expiry verify item is already gone — the code answers it (`maxAge` one year), and I've filled it in and pushed (`4fe62e7f`).

**3. Decisions, not data**
- **Google Analytics**: keep `NEXT_PUBLIC_GA_MEASUREMENT_ID` unset in production, or a GA section *plus a consent banner* become mandatory — a warning comment guards the spot in privacy.mdx.
- **English-only vs. bilingual** legal pages — English is defensible for your audience; German alongside is the risk-averse option.
- **terms.mdx** — still next-forge boilerplate describing accounts that don't exist, and it's live at `/legal/terms` and in the sitemap. My recommendation: delete it now and write real terms when the cohort starts selling; say the word and it's gone.

**How to hand it over:** paste the values here in any form and I'll fill, verify the build, and strip the guidance comments — or edit the two files yourself; every comment deletes cleanly and the brackets are the only things that need touching.

This happens in server logs, on the legal basis of our legitimate interest (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR) in delivering the site securely. Legal basis: legitimate interest (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR) in finding and fixing defects. I'm looking at two build tasks tied to PR #392's branch, starting with redesigning the contact form and page to match the house design system—swapping the next-forge ContactForm for the house grammar (Navbar, rail grid, Subheading/Heading, standfirst, and inputs styled like the Digest form) while keeping the working Resend server action intact.

I need to check how ContactForm currently handles state before rewriting it, likely using useActionState with the same prevState/formData contract, and drop the dictionary dependency in favor of hardcoded English like the other house pages. For the copy, I'm drafting an eyebrow ("Contact") and headline options, weighing something plain and warm in Roach's voice—leaning toward a personal, first-person-adjacent line like "Write to Eric" since the site already uses that voice elsewhere.

I'm settling on "Write to Eric" as the H1, paired with a standfirst describing that questions about chapters, cohorts, or broken things all land in one inbox answered by a human. I'm also considering a MetaAside about the rate limiting, but need to be careful not to overpromise on response times or claim things about the Upstash configuration I'm not certain hold true in production — keeping the aside honest and simple instead.

Now I'm working out the form UI using existing design-system components (Input, Label, Button, Textarea) with stacked fields for name, email, and message, plus a submit button labeled "Send" and pending/success/error states via useActionState. On success I want to swap the form for a short confirmation line rather than anything elaborate, and I'm also noting to add a Contact link to the footer's Playground column.

Now I'm thinking through the unsubscribe flow — I need a tokened link in digest emails (something like /unsubscribe?token=), so I should check how the existing confirm/confirmed routes and Subscriber type handle tokens to mirror that pattern, then build a GET route that looks up the subscriber by token and hard-deletes their record per the stated privacy policy.

I'll need a small styled /unsubscribed confirmation page, and I need to figure out whether existing subscribers already have a stable token I can reuse or whether I need to generate one lazily for unsubscribe purposes. Then I'll wire the unsubscribe link into the digest and welcome email templates using that token.

I still need to find and update whichever sending code dispatches these digest and welcome emails so they pass the unsubscribe URL, and mirror the existing confirm-route tests for this new unsubscribe flow. I also need to check whether /unsubscribed should be excluded from the i18n middleware the same way /confirmed currently is.

content.thinking:
I see that confirmed subscribers get pushed into a Resend Audience, which changes my approach entirely — Resend Audiences have built-in unsubscribe handling, so I can use their unsubscribe URL variable and let Resend manage the one-click unsubscribe flow automatically rather than building it myself.

But there's a data consistency problem: two stores exist (MongoDB and Resend's audience), and the policy promises full deletion, while Resend's native unsubscribe only suppresses the contact rather than deleting it, and MongoDB never finds out. To honor a hard-delete policy, I need my own unsubscribe endpoint that deletes both the Mongo subscriber record and the Resend contact, with emails linking to that endpoint instead of Resend's default. This also means I need a durable per-subscriber secret token for these links since the confirmation token becomes stale after confirming — I'm considering adding a dedicated unsubscribe token field.

The tricky part is that if I store only a hash, the sender can't reproduce the plain token when composing digest emails, so I'm weighing options: storing the plain token directly (common practice for low-sensitivity unsubscribe links) versus deriving it deterministically via HMAC on the email, which would avoid storage but require a new secret. Given the friction of introducing another env variable, the simplest path seems to be generating a random, durable plain unsubscribe token at confirmation time and storing it directly on the subscriber record so the digest sender can read it per recipient.

I'm also questioning whether digests are even sent per-recipient at all, or as a single Resend broadcast to the whole audience -- if it's a broadcast, injecting custom per-contact unsubscribe URLs might not be possible, since broadcasts typically only support merge tags like contact name fields rather than arbitrary per-contact links, which would push me toward relying on Resend's own hosted one-click unsubscribe mechanism instead.

Confirmed subscribers get added to a Resend Audience, which offers native unsubscribe handling for broadcasts and changes the unsubscribe design approach. I'll now check how digests are actually sent before finalizing the design.

--- title: "Privacy Policy" description: "What this site processes, why, on which legal basis, and the rights you have — under the GDPR and the German TDDDG." --- Last updated: 21 August 2026 ## Controller The controller responsible for processing on this website (hastoggle.dev) is: **Ernst Stolz**
Limberger Straße 40
49080 Osnabrück
Germany Email: support@spiritsdontfly.com ## The short version This site has no accounts, no advertising, and no cross-site tracking. Most of it is static pages with running demos. What does get processed: server logs when pages are delivered, cookieless usage statistics, error reports when something breaks, an email address if you sign up for the Monday digest, and whatever you write us through the contact form. One demo sets one cookie, and it says so right next to the button. The details, legal bases and your rights follow below. ## Legal bases Where this policy names a legal basis, it refers to Art. 6 (1) GDPR: - **(a) consent** — you actively agreed, and can withdraw at any time; - **(b) contract** — processing is needed to do the thing you asked for; - **(f) legitimate interest** — running this site securely and reliably. For storing or reading information on your device (cookies, local storage), § 25 TDDDG applies; this site only uses storage that is strictly necessary for a function you use (§ 25 (2) TDDDG), so no consent banner is required. ## Hosting This site is hosted by **Vercel Inc.**, 650 California St, San Francisco, CA 94108, USA. When you open a page, Vercel processes the technical data every web server needs: your IP address, the requested URL, date and time, transferred data volume, referrer, and user-agent. This happens in server logs, on the legal basis of our legitimate interest (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR) in delivering the site securely. Server-side functions run in Vercel's Frankfurt region; static content is delivered by Vercel's global edge network. Vercel is certified under the EU–US Data Privacy Framework, and a data processing agreement is in place ([vercel.com/legal/dpa](https://vercel.com/legal/dpa)). ## Error monitoring When something on the site crashes, an error report is sent to **Sentry** (Functional Software, Inc., 45 Fremont Street, San Francisco, CA 94105, USA), containing the technical context of the error — which may include your IP address, user-agent, and the state of the page at the time. Our Sentry project uses EU data residency, so error data is processed within the European Union; a data processing agreement is in place. Legal basis: legitimate interest (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR) in finding and fixing defects. IP addresses are not used to identify visitors, and error events are retained for 90 days. ## Usage statistics This site uses **Vercel Web Analytics**, which counts page views and interactions without cookies and without persistent identifiers: visitors are distinguished by a short-lived hash that cannot be traced across sites or days. No advertising IDs, no cross-site profiles. Legal basis: legitimate interest (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR) in knowing which pages are read. {/* GOOGLE ANALYTICS — Eric's call, 2026-08-21: no GA. The codebase can load GA when NEXT_PUBLIC_GA_MEASUREMENT_ID is set; if that key is ever set in production, a GA section with consent handling (Art. 6 (1) (a), § 25 (1) TDDDG) and a consent banner become MANDATORY, because GA is not "strictly necessary". Until then this comment is the guard. */} ## Cookies and local storage This site sets exactly one cookie: `playground-presses`, an `httpOnly` cookie holding the press count of the Server Actions demo — it exists so the demo can prove a point about cookies your JavaScript cannot read, and it is functional storage under § 25 (2) TDDDG. It expires after one year and identifies nothing but a number. Your theme choice (light, dark, or system) is kept in your browser's local storage, never sent to us. Fonts are self-hosted; no requests go to font CDNs. ## The Monday digest If you sign up for the weekly email, we process your email address — nothing else — to send you the digest. Signup is double opt-in: you get a confirmation email, and only a confirmed address is ever written to the list. We store the address, the confirmation status, and its timestamps in our database, hosted in the EU (MongoDB Atlas, Frankfurt region); emails are sent through **Resend** (Plus Five Five, Inc., 2261 Market Street #5039, San Francisco, CA 94114, USA) as our processor. Legal basis: your consent (Art. 6 (1) (a) GDPR). Every digest email contains an unsubscribe link; unsubscribing is one click, and your address is then deleted from the list. {/* BEFORE THE FIRST DIGEST SENDS: the unsubscribe flow described above does not exist in the codebase yet — the subscriber model carries an `unsubscribed` flag, but no endpoint and no link in the email templates. It must ship before email one, and it should hard-delete (or at minimum suppress and anonymize) to keep this paragraph true. */} ## Contact form If you write to us through the [contact form](/contact), we process the data you enter — name, email address, and your message — to answer you. Your message reaches us as an email, delivered through Resend to our support inbox. Legal basis: Art. 6 (1) (b) GDPR where your message concerns a contract or pre-contractual question, otherwise our legitimate interest in answering (Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR). Messages are retained as long as the conversation requires, then deleted. ## Recipients and transfers to third countries The processors named above — Vercel, Sentry, and Resend — act on our behalf under data processing agreements. Where processing touches the United States, transfers rest on the EU–US Data Privacy Framework (Vercel and Resend are certified participants) and, where applicable, EU standard contractual clauses; Sentry keeps this site's error data in the EU. We do not sell personal data, and no data is shared for advertising. ## Storage duration Server logs are kept for the hosting provider's technical retention period, error events for 90 days, the digest address until you unsubscribe, and contact messages for the duration of the conversation. Beyond that, personal data is deleted when the purpose it was collected for ends. ## Your rights Under the GDPR you have the right to: - **access** the personal data we hold about you (Art. 15), - **rectification** of inaccurate data (Art. 16), - **erasure** (Art. 17) and **restriction of processing** (Art. 18), - **data portability** (Art. 20), - **object** to processing based on legitimate interest (Art. 21), - **withdraw consent** at any time with effect for the future (Art. 7 (3)) — for the digest, the unsubscribe link is exactly that. To exercise any of these, one email to support@spiritsdontfly.com is enough. You also have the right to lodge a complaint with a data protection supervisory authority, in particular in the member state of your habitual residence. The authority responsible for us is: Die Landesbeauftragte für den Datenschutz Niedersachsen
Prinzenstraße 5
30159 Hannover, Germany
[lfd.niedersachsen.de](https://lfd.niedersachsen.de) ## Changes to this policy This policy is updated when the site's processing changes — for example, when a new chapter of the lab genuinely needs a new mechanism. The current version always lives at this address; the date at the top says when it last moved.

content.thinking: Both changes are pushed now, bringing PR #392 to 33 commits. For the final message, I should summarize both build results, the design contract I uncovered around the Resend audience and our endpoint, the shift to type-level enforcement, and how it was verified — plus flag the required-prop implication for future senders and note that the warn-level lints remain untouched as an accepted class in this repo. I'll keep it concise since it's the end of a long day.

content.text:
Both done, pushed — PR #392 now carries 33 commits.

**The unsubscribe flow (`f01d1e5c`'s first half)** — designed around what the investigation actually found: confirmed subscribers live in *two* stores, your MongoDB and a Resend Audience. So the flow keeps the policy's "deleted" promise literally true in both: confirmation now mints a durable `unsubscribeToken` per subscriber (stored in the clear deliberately — future digest senders must render each recipient's link, and the token grants nothing but removal), and `GET /api/unsubscribe?token=…` **deletes the subscriber document and removes the Resend contact**, then lands on a house-styled `/unsubscribed` page — *"off the list and deleted — not parked."* The route's comment records the contract that matters later: when digest broadcasts get built, they must link *our* endpoint, not Resend's hosted unsubscribe, which only suppresses and would leave your database holding an address the policy says is gone. My favorite piece: the digest template's `unsubscribeUrl` is a **required prop** — a digest email without an unsubscribe link now refuses to compile. The welcome template takes it optionally, the app's preview page passes a placeholder, and the privacy policy's warning comment retired because its paragraph is finally backed by code. Verified: the route 400s without a token, `/unsubscribed` renders (with its i18n-middleware exclusion, mirroring `/confirmed`), 217 tests, clean production build. The full happy path needs a real subscriber in the database — first actual confirm on preview/prod will exercise it.

**The contact page** is out of next-forge and into the house: navbar, rail grid, *Contact* eyebrow, **"Write to Eric."** as the h1, a standfirst in the frame register ("A question about a chapter, something that looks broken, an idea the lab should steal — it all lands in one inbox, and a person answers."), three design-system fields, "Send it," and a mono success line carrying the one useful fact — that replies come from `support@spiritsdontfly.com`. The aside does the hasToggle thing and tells the truth about the mechanism: *a Server Action wired straight to an email inbox — chapter 04's lesson, doing its day job.* The working action is untouched, and the footer's Playground column gained **Contact**, so the imprint's second fast-contact channel is now reachable the ordinary way too. Screenshot-verified.

One housekeeping note: a handful of warn-level Biome findings surfaced in the state chapter's cards during the sweep (`noUnnecessaryConditions` on ref guards, `noJsxPropsBind`) — same accepted-judgment class the repo already carries in the masterclass, exit code clean, so I left them. Copy on the contact page and the two email footers is drafted through the voice passes and, as ever, awaits yours.

content.thinking: Eric flagged three things: misaligned pluses in the footer, a question about whether the logo needs those two pluses since it looks incomplete, and updating the email to eric@hastoggle.dev everywhere it appears. content.text: Reading both screenshots to see exactly which pluses are off.

content.thinking:
I'm examining the copyright box's four plus markers, checking whether the two left-side pluses actually line up on the same x-axis or if there's a subtle vertical offset between the top pair.

Since the item is the first child of its wrapper, it should render all four corner icons at consistent positions—yet the screenshot shows the left pair sitting at a different height than the right pair. The rows have double rules 8px apart, and icons are offset -8px from the item top, so they should straddle the second rule; the mismatch suggests the left and right icons in this crop might actually belong to two separate adjacent items rather than one.

So the left icons sit noticeably lower than the right icons, which is odd if they're all conditional renders from the same item's classes — if the item weren't first-child, the left icons should be hidden entirely rather than just offset. I'm wondering if the right pluses actually belong to a neighboring element instead of this same copyright item, though the crop doesn't show any adjacent text to confirm that.

I think the better approach is to reproduce this locally and actually measure the bounding rects of all four icons rather than guessing from pixels in a screenshot. Separately, the second screenshot of the navbar logo only shows two pluses (top-left, top-right) with the bottom pair missing entirely, which makes sense if the bottom icons are gated by a `group-last/row` class and the navbar's row isn't triggering that condition.

I'm double-checking the row nesting logic — since PlusGridRow is the sole child of PlusGrid, it should count as last-child and trigger the bottom rule/plus rendering regardless of what surrounds the Navbar itself, so the missing bottom rules in the screenshot must come from something else, possibly a dark-mode rendering quirk.

So the bottom rule should be tied to the row being last, and since the navbar has one row it should qualify — yet the screenshot doesn't show it. I recall earlier dark screenshots did clearly show the bottom double rules and corner pluses, so something changed since then.

Looking closer at the crop dimensions, though, the logo appears zoomed roughly 4x, meaning the bottom edge with its rules and pluses likely falls just below the visible crop area. So the missing bottom pluses in this screenshot are probably just an artifact of cropping, not an actual rendering bug — Eric's comment is more about the visual feel of pluses at the logo looking incomplete, not about them being technically absent.

I'm weighing whether to remove the plus icons specifically from the logo item while keeping them elsewhere in the nav and footer, or find another way to make that corner feel more resolved without breaking the grid's visual consistency.

Now I'm digging into the footer misalignment itself — trying to figure out why the corner icons on the copyright box and the socials row don't line up vertically, since both are positioned relative to their own item and should theoretically match unless something from an adjacent row (like the sitemap row above) is bleeding through or being hidden incorrectly.

I should stop guessing and actually measure the exact rectangle of every plus icon in the footer's bottom row directly in the browser.

For the email swap to eric@hastoggle.dev, I need to check imprint, privacy, and the contact form success message, and grep for support@spiritsdontfly.com across content and app. There's a subtlety though — the RESEND_FROM env var controls the actual sending address, separate from what the page copy claims, so if the copy says replies come from support@spiritsdontfly.com but the real send address doesn't match after I change the copy, that's a truth mismatch unless Eric is also updating the environment variable.

My plan going forward: start the server using the existing build since the footer/contact code hasn't changed, measure the footer icon rectangles precisely to diagnose the misalignment, then remove the plus icons from both nav and footer logo items in favor of plain padded divs, swap all page-copy email references, and finally verify everything with screenshots in light and dark mode before committing and pushing.

Both screenshots confirm the offset in the footer's copyright plus pairs and the stray top pluses on the navbar logo—dropping them for cleaner grammar (pluses on interactive boxes, rules for the band) is the right call. Now measuring the footer icons precisely before making changes.

content.text:
All three done, verified, pushed (`8d2afed9`).

**The misaligned pluses** turned out to be an item-height problem, not an icon problem. Measuring the footer's bottom row: the theme pill makes its box 56px tall, but the copyright box sized itself to its text at 48px — so its bottom corner marks hung 8px above the rules the taller boxes sit on. The fix was height, not position: the copyright item now stretches to the row, and the post-fix measurement shows every visible corner mark in the bottom row sitting on exactly two y-positions. The whole utility row now reads as one continuous ledger line — copyright, pill, socials, all cornered on the same rules.

**The logo pluses are gone** — your read was right, and I applied it consistently: two lone marks around a wordmark look like an unfinished frame, so the logo is now a plain padded element in *both* the navbar and the footer. The plus vocabulary belongs exclusively to the interactive boxes (nav links, theme pill, socials, copyright); the logo keeps the rules alone. The footer screenshot confirms the calmer top band.

**Email swapped** to `eric@hastoggle.dev` in all four page occurrences: the imprint's contact section, the privacy policy's controller block and rights section, and the contact form's success line. One operational note that goes with it: the *pages* now advertise that address, but the actual sending identity is the `RESEND_FROM` environment variable in Vercel (it's both the contact form's destination inbox and the digest sender) — for the success line's "replies come from eric@hastoggle.dev" to stay literally true, `RESEND_FROM` should switch to match, and the `eric@hastoggle.dev` mailbox needs to exist and be verified as a Resend sender domain. That's dashboard territory only you can touch.
